findings.claim: Body measurement, pattern measurement and finished garment measurement are three different numbers, and a fitting failure is usually a mistranslation between them rather than a sewing error.
findings.proposed_wording: Body measurement, pattern (flat, seamline-to-seamline) measurement and finished-garment measurement are three different numbers. Body + ease = finished garment; the flat pattern additionally carries seam allowances, darts and overlaps. Many fitting failures are a mistranslation between these three numbers rather than a sewing error — but non-pattern causes (construction, pressing, grain, fabric) are equally documented and must be eliminated before the mistranslation reading is accepted.
findings.notes: The three-number structure is directly supported by E-372, read in full: 'Measure each pattern piece at points that correspond with body measurements'; 'Measure from seamline to seamline'; 'After measuring the body and adding needed ease, compare this measurement to the pattern's measurement. The difference is the amount of alteration needed.' Finished-garment measurements printed separately on tissue/envelope is standard pattern-company practice. What I could NOT verify is the quantifier 'usually'. No source I found ranks mistranslation above construction error as a cause of fitting failure; E-372's own fit checklist and NMSU C-309 both attribute fit faults to construction and pressing. 'Usually' is an unevidenced frequency claim and should be dropped or replaced with 'often'.

findings.claim: A diagnostic toile must be cut in a fabric of similar weight and drape to the intended fabric, otherwise the signs observed belong to the toile fabric rather than to the pattern.
findings.proposed_wording: Toile fabric choice is a real and contested decision, not a settled rule. Match weight, drape and stretch to the fashion fabric when the fault you are hunting is drape-dependent (a drapey design, a knit, a bias cut) — a toile in the wrong fabric class will mislead you. For skeleton fitting of a woven garment — length, width, balance, dart position — a plain, slightly stiff calico or muslin is the long-standing default and is easier to read, because a drapey toile hides the very folds you are trying to see. State which of the two you are doing before you cut.
findings.notes: This claim is written as an absolute ('must ... otherwise') and there is a genuine, documented disagreement. FOR: Tilly and the Buttons — 'Fabric weight, drape, stretch, and stiffness all affect fit. A toile in the wrong type of fabric will give you misleading results'; Seamwork — 'The toile is cut in an inexpensive fabric that closely resembles the hand and drape of the final fashion fabric', 'Cut toiles for knit garments in an inexpensive knit fabric'; Closet Core — 'Your muslin fabric should mimic the fabric you'll use for the final garment'. AGAINST: the repository's OWN cited authority S-0003 (E-372), which I read in full, says only 'make the garment in an inexpensive fabric or pattern-tracing product before cutting out the fashion fabric' — it imposes NO weight/drape requirement, so CC-13 is mis-cited to S-0003. Oliver + S tip 1 is 'Use cheap, somewhat stiff muslin'. The same Closet Core article that recommends matching also cautions against using a truly drapey material for the test garment because drape makes fit hard to assess. And Palmer/Pletsch — a leading fitting authority — dispense with the toile entirely ('There's no need to make a muslin!'), which means the claim's premise is not universal. S-0004 (WSU EM4582) could not be opened, so the second citation could not be checked either.

findings.claim: Centre front, centre back, bust level and waist must be marked on the toile before it is worn, because these lines are the reference against which displacement is read.
findings.proposed_wording: Mark centre front, centre back, the grainlines, and horizontal reference lines at bust, waist and hip on the toile before it is worn. Draw the horizontals perpendicular to the grainline. Read them against the room, not against the garment: horizontals must hang parallel to the floor and verticals perpendicular to it. Marking in a contrasting basting thread rather than pen lets you feel the line as well as see it. (This is standard couture and draping practice; the cooperative-extension publications this book cites do not teach it.)
findings.notes: The practice and the stated purpose are both confirmed by practitioner and draping sources: Closet Core (Susan Khalje method) — 'All pattern marks are transferred to the fabric, including darts, notches, grainlines, center front, center back etc. To assess balance and ensure the grainline and style lines are running in the right direction, I suggest marking bust/waist/hip marks ... and then drawing horizontal lines across the body of the garment at these areas'; draping practice anchors the muslin at centre front on grain and style-tapes bust/waist/hip. Seamwork marks grain plus hip/thigh/knee placements on trouser toiles. IMPORTANT CITATION FAULT: the repo cites S-0003 and S-0004. I read S-0003 (E-372) in full and it contains NO instruction to mark reference lines on a test garment; its only related content is the fit-checklist item 'Lengthwise grainlines, side seams, center front and center back seams hang straight or at right angles to the floor' — i.e. it uses the SEAMS as reference, not drawn lines, and says nothing about bust level or waist. S-0004 could not be opened. The claim is true but is currently attributed to sources that do not say it; its real support is practitioner-level, and confidence is capped at MEDIUM for that reason.

findings.claim: A measurement read from a toile is invalid unless the seam allowance actually sewn is the one the pattern assumed.
findings.proposed_wording: A measurement read from a toile is invalid unless you know where the stitching line is. It is the STITCHING LINE, not the seam allowance width, that must match the pattern: a toile sewn 6 mm off the intended seamline on each of four vertical seams removes about 5 cm of girth and will be misread as a pattern fault. Standard toile practice is the opposite of copying the pattern's seam allowance — cut wider allowances (about 25 mm) at the seams you expect to alter, and mark or thread-trace the true seamline so you can let out as well as take in without losing your reference.
findings.notes: The underlying mechanism is well supported. E-372: 'Measure from seamline to seamline'; and 'If the alteration needed is 1 inch (2.5 cm) or less, alterations often can be made in the existing seam allowances' — i.e. seam-allowance width is directly convertible into garment girth. But the claim as written gives the wrong operational instruction and CONFLICTS with mainstream toile practice, which deliberately uses WIDER allowances: Closet Core — 'Seam allowances are generally larger; Susan suggests 1" which gives you lots of room to make adjustments', with the seamlines machine-stitched in thread; Oliver + S tip 5 — 'Leave extra seam allowances in areas needing adjustment'; Palmer/Pletsch developed their fitting pattern 'with outlets to lengthen the crotch and larger "in case" seam allowances'. A reader who follows CC-15 literally will sew a toile they cannot let out. The claim must be re-anchored on the stitching line rather than on the allowance width.

findings.claim: A fitting is valid only over the undergarments that will be worn with the finished garment.
findings.proposed_wording: Measure and fit over the undergarments that will be worn with the finished garment, and in shoes of the heel height that will be worn with it. Changing bra or shapewear moves the bust apex and the waist level; changing heel height moves the hem, the stance and, for trousers, the crotch. A fitting done in different underwear or different shoes is not comparable with the one before it.
findings.notes: Directly supported at institutional level, but note the sources state it for MEASURING rather than for the fitting session: E-372 — 'Take all measurements snugly, but not tightly, over undergarments usually worn. Also, wear shoes similar to those usually worn.'; NMSU C-227 — 'Measure over the undergarments you will wear with the pants.'; NMSU C-228 measurement table — 'Remove clothing or wear only undergarments'. For the fitting itself the support is practitioner-level: Oliver + S tip 9, 'Wear well-fitting undergarments'. THE OMISSION IS THE PROBLEM: the same authoritative sentence that gives the undergarment rule also gives the FOOTWEAR rule, and footwear appears nowhere in CC-16 nor in the eleven-item confounder list in fit_signs.json, even though CHAPTER_SPECS Bölüm 5 lists 'ayakkabı' among the fitting conditions. The claim should carry both halves of the source sentence.

findings.claim: Movement tests reveal ease shortfalls that are invisible while standing still, so a fitting that never moves is incomplete.
findings.proposed_wording: A fitting that never moves is incomplete. Run five movements and record each as pass/fail: (1) raise both arms overhead; (2) reach both arms straight forward, as if holding a steering wheel, and then fold them across the chest — this is the most demanding test of cross-back width and shoulder fit; (3) bend forward from the waist; (4) sit down on a hard chair and stay seated; (5) take a full stride and, for trousers, climb a step. Sitting and bending test waist, seat, crotch depth and skirt/trouser girth; the arm movements test cross-back, armhole depth and sleeve. Note that ease consumed by movement is the reason wearing ease exists and cannot be seen while standing.
findings.notes: Supported at institutional level, though as an ease criterion rather than as a named protocol. E-372 fit checklist: 'Adequate wearing ease is available for sitting, moving and bending', and for trousers 'The waistband fits the body comfortably and stays in place when bending and sitting.' Practitioner sources give explicit test sets: Seamwork — 'Sit, bend, and wave to test the toile for movement'; Tilly and the Buttons — 'Can you move comfortably? Lift your arms, sit down, walk around'. Apparel-science wear-trial methodology likewise has subjects 'perform a series of activities which normally occur in practice' and rate ease of movement. TWO PROBLEMS WITH THE BOOK'S VERSION. (a) Mis-citation: CC-18 cites S-0001 (NMSU C-228). I read C-228 in full; it contains no movement test and no fitting session at all — only a measurement table and pattern alterations. The correct institutional citation is S-0003. (b) The book's four tests (arm forward, arm raised, sitting, stepping) omit BENDING, which is the one movement E-372 names twice, and they do not include the arms-crossed / reach-forward test that practitioner sources identify as the most demanding single test of back width.

findings.claim: Only one variable may be changed per test, because two simultaneous changes cannot be attributed.
findings.proposed_wording: Change one thing at a time. Authoritative pattern-alteration guidance states the rule directly — 'Make only one alteration at a time' — and the reason the book adds is the standard one: two simultaneous changes cannot be attributed to either. (Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, E-372, Principles of Pattern Alteration.)
findings.notes: The task brief records CC-19 as having NO source. That is a repository error, not a real gap: the project's own S-0003 states the rule verbatim — 'Make only one alteration at a time.' I read the sentence in the full text of E-372. Sewaholic and other practitioner sources repeat it ('take it one at a time'). The only narrowing worth stating is that E-372's rule governs pattern ALTERATIONS, whereas CC-19 governs diagnostic TESTS; the transfer is an obvious and safe analogy, but the book should say which one the source licenses. Action: add source_refs ['S-0003'] to CC-19 in CONCEPTUAL_CLAIMS.json.

findings.claim: The cheapest reversible physical test should always be applied before the pattern is cut, because cutting is not reversible.
findings.proposed_wording: Cutting is not reversible: 'Once the fabric is cut, fitting adjustments are limited to existing darts and seam allowances' (E-372). So work up a ladder of increasingly irreversible tests and stop at the first one that answers the question: pin the tissue or the pattern; pin-baste the fabric with the pins on the outside; machine-baste; stitch; cut last. This escalation is documented practice; the general slogan 'always apply the cheapest reversible test first' is this book's own formulation of it.
findings.notes: The irreversibility premise is stated almost word for word by E-372: 'Once the fabric is cut, however, fitting adjustments are limited to existing darts and seam allowances. Therefore, fitting problems should be solved before the garment is cut by making needed changes in the pattern.' The rungs of the ladder are each documented: NMSU C-228 — 'do a careful pin-fitting to further ensure that your garment will fit well'; E-372 — 'baste only the basic parts of the garment together'; Palmer/Pletsch fabric-fitting order — 'Pin-baste main sections with wrong sides together and try on ... Move pins to improve fit and mark adjusted seamlines ... Stitch darts and seams ... Baste sleeves, try on, then sew.' What I did NOT find in any source is the general economic principle 'cheapest first'. It is a sound generalisation of documented practice but it is the book's own; present it as the book's method rather than as established teaching.

findings.claim: A diagnostic cycle is not complete until the change has been applied and the region re-observed; a sign that is reduced but not gone means a second cause is still present.
findings.proposed_wording: A diagnostic cycle is not complete until the change has been applied and the region re-observed. Iterative re-fitting is documented practice: Palmer/Pletsch run three successive tissue-fittings, each ending 'Note changes. Take off pattern; unpin completely. Alter,' then try on again. If the sign is reduced but not gone, there are two possibilities and you must distinguish them: the cause was right but the AMOUNT was too small, or a second cause is also acting. Test the amount first — increase the same change — because that is the cheaper test; only if a further increase stops helping, or starts producing a new sign elsewhere, treat it as a second cause.
findings.notes: FIRST HALF SUPPORTED. Palmer/Pletsch's published order is literally an apply-and-re-observe loop across three tissue-fittings plus a fabric fit-as-you-sew stage ('Baste sleeves, try on, then sew ... Try on again to mark sleeve and bottom hems'). Rivet Patterns: 'Start small (1/8-1/4") and baste the amount out of your muslin.' SECOND HALF IS A LOGICAL ERROR AND IS UNSUPPORTED. I searched fitting literature for any statement that partial improvement implies a second cause and found none. The inference is invalid: partial reduction is at least as commonly explained by under-correction of the single correct cause — which is exactly what Rivet's 'start small and increment' practice assumes. As written, CC-21 will send readers hunting a second cause when the correct next move is to increase the first change. This is the most consequential reasoning defect I found in my domain.

findings.claim: Eleven ordinary non-pattern conditions can produce fit signs that are indistinguishable from pattern faults, and they must be ruled out before a pattern diagnosis is accepted.
findings.proposed_wording: A group of ordinary non-pattern conditions produces fit signs that are easily MISTAKEN for pattern faults, and they must be ruled out before a pattern diagnosis is accepted. Fix one number for this list and use it in every chapter. State plainly which items rest on cooperative-extension authority (fabric, grain/cutting, pressing, seam allowance, size choice, undergarments, measurement accuracy) and which are this book's own additions from current home-sewing practice (PDF print scale, fitting posture as an observation artefact, design ease misread as excess).
findings.notes: PER-ITEM CHECK against authority. (1) Fabric — SUPPORTED, E-372's opening: 'Standards of good fit are influenced by many things such as the current fashion look, the hang and stretch of the fabric, the amount of ease preferred and figure size and type'; Tilly: 'Fabric weight, drape, stretch, and stiffness all affect fit.' (2) Cutting off-grain — SUPPORTED, E-372: 'For garments to hang and fit correctly, the lengthwise grain of the fabric must lie at a right angle to the floor along major parts of the body'; C-227 lists 'Pressed creases that hang off-grain' as a fault to avoid. (3) Pressing — SUPPORTED, NMSU C-309: 'Pressing incorrectly can pull fabric out of line ... It will flatten curves, stretch the neckline, ripple the skirt hem, and generally change the shape of the garment.' (4) Seam allowance — SUPPORTED, E-372: alterations of 1 inch or less 'often can be made in the existing seam allowances', i.e. allowance width converts directly into girth. (5) Size choice — SUPPORTED, E-372 high-bust rule and C-227 'select a pattern size according to measurements at the fullest part of your hips'. (6) Undergarments — SUPPORTED (E-372, C-227, C-228). (7) Measurement — SUPPORTED, E-372: 'Accurate measurements are the key to good fit.' (8) Construction — SUPPORTED_NARROWER; no single source enumerates uneven allowance / stretched edge / omitted interfacing as a diagnostic confounder, though each is documented separately (C-309 on stretching; C-228 on interfacing selection). (9) Ease misread as excess — SUPPORTED_NARROWER; the wearing/design ease split is universal, but no source frames it as a diagnostic confounder. (10) PDF print scale — SUPPORTED at practitioner level only; no institutional source. (11) Fitting posture — SUPPORTED_NARROWER; C-227 treats posture as a BODY variation (average / forward-tilted hip / backward-tilted hip) that legitimately changes the pattern, which is not the same thing as the reader adopting an unnatural stance during the fitting. Only tailoring-practice sources address the latter. NONE OF THE ELEVEN IS UNSUPPORTED. TWO STRUCTURAL FAULTS, both internal and both verifiable by command. (a) COUNT CONTRADICTION: fit_signs.json yields exactly 11 classes, but DIAGNOSTIC_SYSTEM.md § 3 ① says 'dokuz kalem', CHAPTER_SPECS Bölüm 8 says 'dokuz nedeni' and lists nine by name, and SOURCE_MAP.md § 1 row C-H says '9'. Three documents say nine, the claim and the data say eleven. (b) NOT OPERATIONALISED: no sign carries all eleven. Distribution across the 43 signs is Kumaş 40, Beden 31, Prova duruşu 27, Yapım 26, Kesim 17, Ütü 8, İç giyim 7, Kalıp basımı 5, Dikiş payı 4, Ease 2, Ölçüm 1; each individual sign lists only 3–5. A reader working sign-by-sign is never asked to rule out eleven. Underwear is asked for on only 7 of 43 signs although bust apex and waist level move with it. Also note the file's own verification_summary: technical_reference_verified 0/43. (c) 'INDISTINGUISHABLE' is stronger than any source supports; sources say these conditions cause poor fit, not that the resulting signs cannot be told apart from pattern faults. Use 'easily mistaken for'.

findings.claim: A pattern printed at home must be verified against its printed test square before any measurement is taken from it.
findings.proposed_wording: Before any measurement is taken from a home-printed pattern, print the test-square page alone, with printer scaling set to 100% / Actual Size (never Fit to Page), and measure the square in BOTH directions — some printers scale differently along and across the paper. Treat a deviation up to about 1 mm on a 50 mm square (about 2%) as printer accuracy; anything larger, reprint at an adjusted custom scale and measure again. The test square proves the SCALE of one page; it does not prove the ASSEMBLY. After taping, check a long dimension that crosses several page joins against the pattern's stated measurement, because overlap and taping error accumulates independently of print scale.
findings.notes: The practice is universal across PDF pattern publishers and is a genuine, checkable step, so the claim is right. Two honest limits. (a) NO AUTHORITATIVE TOLERANCE EXISTS. I searched for a standards-body, institutional or pattern-industry tolerance and found none. The best-sourced statements are practitioner: Andrie Designs says the square 'is imperative that this square measures exactly 2"' and gives no tolerance, recommending scale adjustment 'by only a few percentage points at a time'; other pattern publishers say a deviation of about 1 mm 'could simply be the limits of your printer's accuracy'. The 1 mm figure in my proposed wording is practitioner convention, and the book must label it as such rather than imply a standard. (b) The claim as written under-specifies the check in two ways that matter: single-axis measurement misses anisotropic printer scaling, and the test square is silent about cumulative page-assembly error. See missing_confounders. Note also that CC-27 has an empty source_refs array; the honest fix is to cite pattern-publisher practice explicitly, not to leave it bare.

findings.claim: Adjustments have a required order: length before width, upper body before lower, bodice before sleeve, armhole settled before the sleeve cap, crotch depth before crotch curve.
findings.proposed_wording: Four of the five ordering rules are established; one is contested. RULE 1, length before width — established: 'Begin with lengthwise alterations at the shoulder or neck and work down. Finish with the alterations for width' (E-372). RULE 3, bodice before sleeve, and RULE 4, armhole settled before the sleeve cap — established, because the sleeve cap is derived from the finished armhole: altering the armscye forces a matching change to the cap. RULE 5, crotch depth before crotch curve — established in the narrower form the source states: 'Alter pattern crotch depth first because it affects crotch length' (NMSU C-227). RULE 2, upper body before lower, is NOT universal. E-372 works top-down; Palmer/Pletsch instead order by dependency — 'DO FIRST ONLY WHAT AFFECTS OTHER AREAS OF FIT. DO LAST WHAT DOESN'T' — and on that rule they fit hip width before shoulder width and require 'Sway/flat/erect back — don't check this until hip width is correct.' State top-down as the default and dependency as the tie-breaker, and say which authority each comes from.
findings.notes: RULE-BY-RULE. (1) LENGTH BEFORE WIDTH — SUPPORTED. E-372 verbatim: 'Make only one alteration at a time. Begin with lengthwise alterations at the shoulder or neck and work down. Finish with the alterations for width, again beginning at the neck and working down.' In House Patterns teaches the same with a middle tier: 'length first, contour second, and width/girth last'. I searched specifically for a source teaching width before length and found none. The one possible dissent is Palmer/Pletsch's terse 'Do vertical before horizontal alterations!', whose meaning turns on their naming convention (they name an alteration by the direction of its slash line, so 'vertical' there plausibly means a width change) — I could not resolve the ambiguity from the excerpt and do not claim it as a contradiction. (2) UPPER BEFORE LOWER — CONTESTED, and this is the finding. E-372 supports it twice ('work down', and 'Many problems in side seams, bust area or length disappear when the pattern is correctly fitted in the neck and shoulder area'). But Palmer/Pletsch's published fitting order does NOT run top-down: its governing rule is dependency, and in their sequence Hip width is settled in the SECOND tissue-fitting while Shoulder width and position is settled in the THIRD, and sway/flat/erect back is explicitly gated on hip width being correct first. A rule presented in Chapter 16 as 'required' is therefore not required by one of the field's most-taught methods. (3) BODICE BEFORE SLEEVE and (4) ARMHOLE BEFORE SLEEVE CAP — SUPPORTED, but the best sources are practitioner and drafting-technical, not extension. Melly Sews: to draft the sleeve 'You'll need some measurements from your bodice pattern — specifically your armscye lengths and armscye depth', and 'When you alter an armscye, you also have to alter the sleeve cap.' Palmer/Pletsch's fabric-fitting order sews and fits the bodice, then 'Baste sleeves, try on, then sew.' Palmer/Pletsch independently support armhole-first for a different reason: 'if you alter the armhole depth, it will affect the height of a horizontal bust dart. So alter the armhole first.' (5) CROTCH DEPTH BEFORE CROTCH CURVE — SUPPORTED_NARROWER. NMSU C-227 footnote 2 to the measurement chart, read in the PDF: 'Alter pattern crotch depth first because it affects crotch length.' The source says depth before LENGTH; the book says depth before CURVE. Crotch length is measured along the crotch curve so the extension is reasonable, but the book should quote the source's own term and not silently upgrade it. Note the internal mapping in DIAGNOSIS_TO_ADJUSTMENT_MAP § 6 states rule 5 as 'AF-15 → AF-16', while SOURCE_MAP § 4 records that AF-16 'is not isolated from AF-15' in any source — so the ordering constraint is asserted between two families the project itself cannot separate.

findings.claim: An adjustment is only reusable if its amount was recorded as a number; 'a bit more' cannot be transferred to the next pattern.
findings.proposed_wording: An adjustment is only reusable if the amount survives the session in a form you can apply again — either as a number written down, or carried physically on a preserved altered pattern. Authoritative practice is the physical record: 'If you make any changes, mark them on the pattern so it will be correct the next time you use it' (NMSU C-227), and 'Preserve the altered pattern for later use' (E-372). This book asks for the number as well, because a number transfers to a DIFFERENT pattern and a marked-up pattern piece does not. The written fit profile is this book's own structure and does not rest on an external source.
findings.notes: The reuse principle is institutionally supported, but in a materially different form from the claim. Every authority I read records the amount ON THE PATTERN, not as a written number: C-227 'mark them on the pattern so it will be correct the next time you use it'; E-372 'Preserve the altered pattern for later use by fusing nonwoven stabilizer on the pattern's wrong side or redraw the pattern and new markings onto pattern paper'; Oliver + S tip 15 'Transfer alterations back to the paper pattern after fitting'; Tilly 'Take measurements on the toile showing where you made changes ... Mark the same change positions on your pattern copy.' The strict claim 'only reusable if recorded as a NUMBER' is therefore false as stated — a preserved altered pattern is reusable and carries the amount geometrically. The book's real and defensible point is narrower: only a number is PORTABLE ACROSS PATTERNS. CHAPTER_SPECS Bölüm 17 already concedes 'Kaynak kanıtı: Yok'; the claim text should concede the same rather than asserting a general rule.

findings.claim: An adjustment that is required on every pattern is evidence about the body rather than about any one pattern, and that is the condition under which drafting a personal block becomes worthwhile.
findings.proposed_wording: An adjustment that recurs across patterns from MORE THAN ONE pattern company is evidence about the body rather than about any one pattern. Within a single company it is not: every house drafts from its own block, so the same alteration recurring on every pattern from one brand is evidence about that brand's block, and the cheaper remedy is to alter that company's fitting shell once and reuse it. Two or more independent drafting systems demanding the same change, in the same direction, by a comparable amount, is the condition under which a personal block earns its cost — and even then it is a choice, not a necessity: established fitting authorities work productively for a lifetime without one.
findings.notes: IS IT DEFENSIBLE OR A SALES ARGUMENT? Both — it is a real inference with a real confounder that the claim does not control for, and the uncontrolled version is what makes it read as a sales argument for Book 3. SUPPORT: the sloper rationale is standard — 'If you make a personalized block to fit your individual figure, clothing made from that block will be a better fit than clothing made from a standard block, especially if you vary from the standard in a large way and/or in a number of ways' (Dresspatternmaking). Practitioner sources add that a sloper is a durable personal record you only make once absent major weight change. THE CONFOUNDER THE CLAIM MISSES: a pattern company's patterns are drafted from that company's own sloper, so once you know how to make that sloper fit, the same alterations apply to all of that company's patterns. Repetition within one brand is therefore fully explained by the brand's block and says nothing about the body. Since most home sewers buy heavily from one or two houses, the claim's antecedent will be satisfied routinely for a brand-block reason, and the book would send the reader to Book 3 on that evidence. This is a correctable defect: require independent drafting systems. COUNTER-AUTHORITY ON THE CONCLUSION: Palmer/Pletsch, one of the most-taught fitting methods, is built expressly to avoid drafting — 'There's no need to draft every design from scratch!', 'There's no need to make a muslin!' — and their whole answer to repeated alterations is to keep altering tissue, not to draft a block. So 'drafting a personal block becomes worthwhile' is a contested recommendation, not a settled one, and the book should not present it as the only rational response to repetition. CC-31 currently has empty source_refs; as written it is the series bridge carrying no evidence and one live confounder.

missing_confounders.name: Garment not supported or not closed during the fitting (no waist string/stay; opening only loosely pinned)
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: An unsupported or unfastened toile hangs from the wrong level. The whole garment then reads as short at the front, long at the back, or twisted, and the reader diagnoses balance, crotch depth or sway back. This is the single most mechanical false-sign generator in a fitting session and it is absent from all eleven classes.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: NMSU C-227, fitting the pants: 'Pin the opening and tie a string snugly around your waistline to hold the pants up ... Observe the fit in a full-length mirror, and adjust the pants from the waistline until the legs hang straight'. E-372, for measuring: 'A string tied around the waist and the base of the neck helps establish reference points.' Palmer/Pletsch fabric-fitting order: 'If there is no waistline seam, insert a zipper in center back before fitting.'

missing_confounders.name: Footwear / heel height at the fitting
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: Heel height changes hem level, pelvic tilt and stance, and for trousers the crotch and leg hang. The book already lists 'ayakkabı' among Chapter 5 fitting conditions but it is not one of the eleven eliminable causes, so a reader working the Chapter 8 checklist never rules it out. Its absence directly weakens CC-29 (hem read last) and every trouser sign.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: E-372: 'Take all measurements snugly, but not tightly, over undergarments usually worn. Also, wear shoes similar to those usually worn.' The undergarment rule the book DID take and the footwear rule it did NOT take are the same sentence in the source.

missing_confounders.name: Fabric not allowed to hang and relax before the hem or vertical measurements are read (bias, loose weaves, heavy crepes, knits)
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: Bias and loosely woven pieces drop after construction. Read too early, the hem is level and then goes uneven, or is uneven and gets 'corrected' into a permanent fault. This produces exactly the signs the book routes to balance and length faults, and it is the most likely non-pattern cause of the uneven-hem sign that CC-29 governs.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: Standard instruction is to hang a bias garment at least 24 hours after the main seams are sewn and before hemming, because the bias drops and the hem is otherwise cut uneven. NOTE: the Threads URL returned HTTP 403 and I read only the search-engine summary; the Seamwork tutorial page was likewise not fetched directly. Treat this item as practitioner consensus that the book should verify against a text it can hold.

missing_confounders.name: Stale measurements — body changed since the measuring session
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: This is the project's own CC-07, but it is not in the elimination list, so it is never applied at the point of decision. A reader whose measurements are eight months old will find real differences between body and pattern and attribute them to the pattern. 'Measuring' as a confounder in fit_signs.json covers method error, not staleness, and it appears on exactly 1 of 43 signs.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: E-372: 'Accurate measurements are the key to good fit. Measurements should be taken at least every 6 months and/or when weight or the figure has varied significantly.' NMSU C-228: 'As time passes, you may find that the problems of fitting your figure may change.'

missing_confounders.name: PDF page assembly / taping error (cumulative), distinct from print-scale error
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: The test square proves the scale of one page and proves nothing about assembly. Overlap, trim and taping error accumulates across page joins, so a correctly printed pattern can still be a centimetre or more wrong across a large piece — and this error is not uniform, so it deforms shape as well as size. The book's 'Kalıp basımı' class explicitly names only the test square, so it certifies a pattern the reader has not actually verified.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: PDF assembly guidance from pattern publishers acknowledges that misalignment and cutting/taping errors stack up across a multi-page tile until the assembled piece is visibly off. I did not fetch the Last Stitch page directly; this is from the search-result summary. The fix is cheap and checkable and should be added regardless: after taping, measure one long dimension crossing several joins against the pattern's own stated measurement.

missing_confounders.name: Anisotropic printer scaling — the test square is measured on one axis only
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: Some printers and drivers scale differently along and across the paper, so a square measured only left-to-right can pass while the pattern is short vertically. Vertical scale error is exactly the error the book's length-first ordering is most sensitive to. This is a defect inside an existing confounder rather than a new one, but it makes that confounder's test unsound as written.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: Published test-square troubleshooting assumes the square is checked as a square (both dimensions) and that scale is corrected by custom-scale percentage. No source I found states a two-axis rule explicitly, so present this as the book's own hardening of the check rather than as cited practice.

missing_confounders.name: Fabric not preshrunk / shrinkage after washing or pressing
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: Present in the data but not as a class: 'Kumaş: yıkama/ütü sonrası çekme' appears on exactly 1 of 43 signs. Steam-pressing during construction shrinks many fabrics, so a toile that fitted before pressing is tight after it, and the fault is read as girth. It deserves either promotion to its own class or attachment to every girth and length sign.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: NMSU C-309 on pressing changing garment shape; Oliver + S deliberately does NOT prewash muslin (tip 1) precisely because prewashing changes the toile's dimensions relative to the fashion fabric — i.e. the shrinkage variable is consciously managed by practitioners.

missing_confounders.name: The observer — self-fitting artefact, and fitting on a dress form instead of the body
missing_confounders.why_it_matters: Looking down at your own bodice, or twisting to see the back in a mirror, changes shoulder and spine position and creates the very drag lines being recorded. A dress form padded to your measurements still has different posture and flesh compliance. The book's 'Prova duruşu' class covers the sitter's posture; it does not cover the act of observing changing the posture, and CHAPTER_SPECS Bölüm 5 anticipates a reader with no helper.
missing_confounders.source_evidence: E-372: 'Have someone help you check the fit of the garment or stand in front of a full-length mirror.' Oliver + S tip 10 recommends being photographed from all sides in natural light rather than relying on your own view. Photographs are the cheap control for this artefact and the book should require them.

top_risks.why: The second half — 'a sign that is reduced but not gone means a second cause is still present' — is a logical error with no source. Partial improvement is at least as often under-correction of the single correct cause. Printed as method, it sends readers hunting an imaginary second cause instead of increasing the change they already made, and it will manufacture spurious diagnoses in Chapters 9–15.

As written it instructs the reader to sew the toile at the pattern's seam allowance. Mainstream toile practice does the opposite — wider allowances with the seamline marked — precisely so the garment can be let out. A reader who follows CC-15 literally builds a toile that cannot answer the question it was made for. The real rule is about the stitching line, not the allowance width.

The series bridge to Book 3 rests on an inference with an uncontrolled confounder and no source. Every pattern from one company derives from that company's block, so 'this alteration is needed on every pattern' is routinely satisfied for a brand-block reason and says nothing about the body. Uncorrected, this is exactly the sales argument the risk_note fears. It becomes defensible with one added condition: recurrence across independent drafting systems.

Rule 2 (upper body before lower) is presented as 'required' and drives both Chapter 16 and the handoff to Book 2, but Palmer/Pletsch's published order contradicts it — hip width before shoulder width, sway back gated on hip width — under a different governing rule ('do first only what affects other areas of fit'). Rule 5 also silently upgrades the source's 'crotch length' to 'crotch curve'.

The count is internally contradictory: three specification documents say nine, the claim and the data say eleven. Worse, the eleven are not operationalised — each sign lists only 3–5, so the reader is never actually asked to run the full elimination that CC-25 says is mandatory. The list is also missing at least two high-frequency false-sign generators (unsupported/unfastened garment at the waist; footwear).

Written as an absolute rule on a genuinely contested question, and mis-cited to S-0003, which says only 'an inexpensive fabric or pattern-tracing product'. Recognised teachers recommend a stiff plain calico for skeleton fitting, and one leading method rejects the toile entirely. Chapter 4's central decision point ('Bu kumaş prova için uygun mu?') is therefore built on an overstated premise.

The claim is sound but the two cited authorities do not support it — E-372 (read in full) contains no toile-marking instruction at all, and S-0004 could not be opened to check. The evidence that does exist is couture/draping practice. The citation must be corrected or the claim relabelled as practitioner convention, or the book asserts institutional backing it does not have.

could_not_verify: WSU Extension EM4582 'Challenging Patterns' (Ettl) — the repository's S-0004 and a cited source for CC-13, CC-14, CC-17, CC-22, CC-23, CC-24, CC-26, CC-29. The only copy I could locate is an expiring signed Amazon S3 link from the WSU library, which returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl; the WSU research-portal URL returns a JavaScript shell. I therefore could NOT verify any claim attributed to S-0004. Only the search-engine summary of its grain sentence was visible ('lengthwise grain perpendicular to the floor, crosswise grain parallel to the floor'). This is material: S-0004 is the book's most-cited authority for the observation and sign-reading chapters, and no reviewer working from the open web can currently check it. Acquire a stable copy.

Threads Magazine articles ('To Get the Right Armhole, Fit the Bodice'; 'Use a Sloper to Alter Patterns'; 'Before You Hem a Bias Garment, Let the Fabric Hang Out'; 'Proper Fitting for a Forward Shoulder'). Every threadsmagazine.com URL returned HTTP 403 behind a Cloudflare challenge to both WebFetch and curl with a browser user-agent. I saw only search-engine summaries and have marked every use of them as such; none is load-bearing for a SUPPORTED verdict.

Iowa State University Extension 'State 4-H Awardrobe Clothing Event — Checklist for Ready-to-Wear' (HTTP 403). This appeared in search results to contain institutional movement-check language ('Will you be bending over? If so, try it in front of the mirror'), which would have raised CC-18's movement tests from practitioner to institutional support. Not obtained.

Seamwork/Colette help-centre article on the test square (HTTP 403). No institutional or standards-body tolerance for home-printed pattern scale was found anywhere; the 1 mm figure in the CC-27 proposed wording is practitioner convention only.

Liechty, Rasband & Pottberg-Steineckert, 'Fitting and Pattern Alteration: A Multi-Method Approach' (Bloomsbury/Fairchild) — the standard university textbook for this exact subject, and the natural authority for the five fit standards (grain, set, line, balance, ease), for adjustment ordering and for figure-variation classification. Not open access; I confirmed only its bibliographic record and scope (88 figure variations). Acquiring it would settle CC-28 rule 2 and much of CC-25 far better than anything on the open web.

Whether the eleven confounders can actually be distinguished from pattern faults in practice — the word 'indistinguishable' in CC-25 and the discriminating-evidence layer beneath it. This is REQUIRES_PHYSICAL_TEST and the repository already says so (SOURCE_MAP § 1 row C-H, DIAGNOSTIC_SYSTEM § 6.4).
ISO 8559-1 and ASTM D5219 were not consulted for this domain; they govern measurement definitions and body dimensions, not fitting protocol, so they would not settle any claim in this brief.
